readerTitle: Why the best salespeople talk less on the first call
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Neil Rackham·Huthwaite의 영업 통화 관찰 연구) + 가상 적용 (포장 기계 공급사, 병원 예약 소프트웨어)
insight: 좋은 영업은 제품 설명이 아니라, 고객이 겪는 문제와 그 문제가 치르게 하는 비용을 고객의 말로 먼저 듣는 데서 시작한다.
misconception: 고객이 원하는 것을 이미 말했으니 바로 견적과 데모를 보내는 것이 가장 빠르고 친절한 영업이다.

sources.text: Huthwaite의 영업 통화 관찰 연구 (Rackham, 1988에 소개)
포장 기계 공급사와 병원 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: "약 35,000건의 영업 통화"와 "12년"은 SPIN Selling 서문과 1장에 나오는 수치입니다. 국가 수 등 세부 수치는 판본마다 다르게 인용되므로 카드에는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
"큰 거래에서는 마무리 압박 기법이 성공률을 떨어뜨렸고, 성과가 좋은 영업사원은 문제의 결과와 해결 가치를 묻는 질문을 더 많이 했다"는 요약은 Rackham(1988)의 핵심 결론입니다. 정확한 비율 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.
5번 카드의 '작은 거래에서는 압박 기법이 통하기도 했다'는 Rackham의 저가·단순 거래 관찰을 일반적으로 요약한 것입니다. 표현을 원문과 대조하세요.

cards.title: Why the best salespeople talk less on the first call
body: Over about 12 years, researchers at a firm called Huthwaite, led by Neil Rackham, studied roughly 35,000 real sales calls.
They expected to find that great sellers had great pitches. What set the best ones apart happened before the pitch.

image.label: A seller listening while a customer talks and points at a whiteboard
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의실에서 고객이 화이트보드의 공정 그림을 가리키며 말하고, 영업 담당자는 노트를 들고 듣는 장면. 영업 담당자의 말풍선은 작고 고객의 말풍선은 크게. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: A warehouse asks for a faster machine.
body: You sell pallet-wrapping machines. A distribution warehouse manager emails: "Our wrapper is too slow. Send me a quote for your fastest model."
Your fastest model is also your most expensive. What do you do first?

options.text: Send the quote today with a good discount
options.feedback: You look fast and helpful. But you're betting the manager has diagnosed the problem correctly, and you compete on price alone.

options.text: Book a demo of the fastest model
options.feedback: A demo builds interest, but it's still about your machine. You don't yet know what "too slow" is costing them.

options.text: Ask for a call to understand what the slow wrapping is causing
options.feedback: It delays the quote by a day or two. In return you learn the real problem, and whether your fastest model even solves it.

cards.title: The problem wasn't speed.
body: On the call, you ask what happens when wrapping falls behind. The manager explains: workers rush, wrap loosely, and pallets arrive at a big retail customer damaged.
That retailer charges a penalty for every damaged load. The penalties are the real pain.
A faster machine might help. But better film tension and a simple load check might help more, for a fraction of the price. Now you can offer the right fix, and the manager trusts you.

image.label: A loosely wrapped pallet tipping over next to a penalty notice
image.brief: 창고 바닥. 느슨하게 감긴 팔레트 화물이 기울어져 있고, 옆에 "Damage penalty"라고 적힌 종이가 붙어 있음. 반대편에는 단단히 감긴 팔레트. 실제 상표 없음.

cards.title: Discovery
body: **Discovery** is the part of a sale where you learn the customer's situation, their problem, what that problem costs them, and what a good result would look like, before you propose anything.

Customers often arrive with a solution in mind, like "a faster machine." Discovery finds the problem underneath it. That lets you sell what actually helps, and lets the customer see the value in their own words.

cards.title: What the 35,000 calls showed
body: Rackham's team found that in small, simple sales, pushy closing tricks sometimes worked. In larger sales, they often backfired.
The sellers who won bigger deals asked more questions. Above all, they asked about **consequences**: what the problem leads to, and what solving it would be worth.
When a customer says out loud, "those penalties cost us every month," the price of a fix starts to look small next to it.

cards.title: Questions that go one layer deeper
body: Good discovery moves from facts to stakes:
list: **Situation:** How do you handle this today?
**Consequence:** What does that lead to? Who feels it?
**Payoff:** If it were fixed, what would change for you?
cards.callout: Most sellers stop at the second layer. The value lives in the last two.

cards.title: Discovery is not an interrogation.
body: Don't ask what you could look up yourself. It wastes the customer's time and shows you didn't prepare.
Match the depth to the purchase. Someone buying a bag of screws doesn't want twenty questions. A few good ones may be enough.
And only ask if you'll use the answers. Asking careful questions and then pitching the same standard package anyway destroys the trust discovery is meant to build.

cards.title: Now it's clinic software.
body: You sell scheduling software for small medical clinics. A clinic manager opens the call: "We need online booking. Can you show me yours?"
What's your best next move?

options.text: Show the online booking feature right away
options.feedback: It answers the request and keeps things moving. But you won't know if booking is the real problem or just the manager's first guess.

options.text: Ask what happens today when patients can't book online, and what that costs the clinic
options.feedback: You might learn the real pain is no-shows or staff stuck on the phone. Then you can show the features that fix it, in the manager's own terms.

options.text: Send a 30-question form to fill in before any demo
options.feedback: You'd gather lots of facts, but you'd turn a warm lead into homework. Many busy managers would simply not reply.

cards.title: Find the problem and its cost before you offer the fix.
body: Customers often ask for a solution. Your job is to learn the problem beneath it and what it costs them.
**Try it today:** before your next sales conversation, write down one question about what the customer's problem *leads to*. Ask it, then stay quiet and listen.
